'''Lisa Marie Piccirillo''' (born 1990 or 1991)<ref name="BG">''The Boston Globe'' [https://www.bostonglobe.com/2020/08/20/magazine/math-problem-stumped-experts-50-years-this-grad-student-maine-solved-it-days/ A math problem stumped experts for 50 years. This grad student from Maine solved it in days ], August 20, 2020; print title: "A Tough Knot to Crack," ''The Boston Globe Magazine'' (August 23, 2020), pp. 23-25.</ref> is an American mathematician specializing in [[low-dimensional topology]]. She is a Professor and holds the Sid W. Richardson Foundation Regents Chair in Mathematics at the [[University of Texas at Austin]].<ref name="UTexasProfile">{{Cite web |title=Lisa Piccirillo|work=Directory |url=https://math.utexas.edu/directory/lisa-piccirillo |access-date=2025-11-19 |publisher=University of Texas Mathematics Department}}</ref> She is known for solving a long-standing problem in [[knot theory]] by proving that the [[Conway knot]] is not [[Slice knot#Slice knots and the knot concordance group|smoothly slice]].<ref name="Annals">{{Cite journal|last=Piccirillo|first=Lisa|date=2020|title=The Conway knot is not slice|journal=Annals of Mathematics|volume=191|issue=2|pages=581–591|doi=10.4007/annals.2020.191.2.5|jstor=10.4007/annals.2020.191.2.5|issn=0003-486X|arxiv=1808.02923|s2cid=52398890}}</ref><ref name="Klarreich">{{Cite web|title=Graduate Student Solves Decades-Old Conway Knot Problem|url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/graduate-student-solves-decades-old-conway-knot-problem-20200519/|last=Klarreich|first=Erica|authorlink=Erica Klarreich |website=[[Quanta Magazine]]|language=en|access-date=May 20, 2020}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Piccirillo was raised in [[Greenwood, Maine]], and attended [[Telstar Regional High School]] in [[Bethel, Maine]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.sunjournal.com/2009/05/15/telstar-regional-high-school/|title=Telstar Regional High School Class of 2009|date=May 15, 2009 |website=Sun Journal |accessdate=2020-08-26}}</ref> Her mother was a middle school math teacher. As a child, her hobbies included riding [[dressage]], church youth group activities, drama, and band.<ref name="BG" />

She earned a B.S. in mathematics from [[Boston College]] in 2013 and a PhD in low-dimensional topology at the [[University of Texas at Austin]] under the supervision of [[John Edwin Luecke]] in 2019.<ref name="thesis">{{cite web|url=https://repositories.lib.utexas.edu/bitstream/handle/2152/75668/PICCIRILLO-DISSERTATION-2019.pdf|title=Knot traces and the slice genus|author=Lisa Marie Piccirillo}}</ref> Boston College professor [[Elisenda Grigsby]] noted Piccirillo's creativity as a key to her success, adding that Piccirillo did not fit the mold of a "standard golden child math prodigy" during her undergraduate studies.<ref name="Klarreich" />

==Career==
After earning her doctorate, Piccirillo was a postdoctoral researcher at [[Brandeis University]].<ref name="cv">{{cite web|url=https://sites.google.com/view/lpiccirillo/research/cv?authuser=0|title=Curriculum vitae|accessdate=May 19, 2020}}</ref> Following the publication of her proof on the Conway knot, she was offered a tenure-track position at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]], where she served as an assistant professor of mathematics from 2020 to 2024.<ref name="MIT-WIM">{{Cite web |title=Lisa Piccirillo Solves Decades-Old Conway Knot Problem – Women In Math |url=https://math.mit.edu/wim/2020/05/20/lisa-piccirillo-solves-decades-old-conway-knot-problem/ |access-date=May 20, 2020 |website=math.mit.edu}}</ref> In 2024, she returned to the University of Texas at Austin as a full professor.<ref name="UTexasProfile"/>

===The Conway knot problem===
[[File:Conway knot.png|thumb|The Conway Knot]]
The Conway knot is named after its discoverer, English mathematician [[John Horton Conway]], who first described it in 1970. While the knot was determined to be [[topologically slice]] in the 1980s, the question of whether it was [[Slice knot#Slice knots and the knot concordance group|smoothly slice]] remained unanswered for fifty years, becoming a famous unsolved problem in knot theory.<ref name="Klarreich" /><ref name="Blakemore">{{Cite news|title=Graduate student untangles nature of Conway knot|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/science/graduate-student-untangles-nature-of-conway-knot/2020/05/22/9a38bebe-9ace-11ea-ac72-3841fcc9b35f_story.html|last=Blakemore|first=Erin |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |language=en|access-date=May 26, 2020}}</ref>

Piccirillo's proof, developed while she was a graduate student, completed the classification of slice knots with fewer than 13 crossings.<ref name="Annals" /> Her work was hailed for its creative methodology; instead of attacking the problem directly, she constructed a "trace" of the Conway knot and found a different knot that shared this trace but was already known not to be smoothly slice. This novel approach demonstrated that the Conway knot was also not slice and, according to ''The Washington Post'', "could point to new ways to understand knots."<ref name="Blakemore" />

Piccirillo learned of the problem at a [https://web.ma.utexas.edu/conferences/gompf/? 2018 conference] and reportedly found the solution in less than a week.<ref name="Klarreich" /> In an interview, she described her initial approach to the problem:

<blockquote>I think the next day, which was a Sunday, I just started trying to run the approach for fun and I worked on it a bit in the evenings just to try to see what's supposed to be hard about this problem.<ref name="Blakemore" /></blockquote>
A few days later, she met with [[Cameron Gordon (mathematician)|Cameron Gordon]], a professor at UT Austin (a senior topologist), and casually mentioned her solution.<ref name="Quanta-Vid" /> Reflecting on the nature of her discovery in an interview with ''[[Quanta Magazine]]'', Piccirillo noted the specificity of her proof in a field that often favors broad generalizations:
<blockquote>It was quite surprising to me. I mean, it's just one knot. In general, when mathematicians prove things, we like to prove really broad, general statements: All objects like this have some property. And I proved like, one knot has a thing. I don't care about knots. So, I do care about three and four dimensional spaces, though. And it turns out that, when you want to study three and four dimensional spaces, you find yourself studying knots anyway...<ref name="Quanta-Vid">{{Cite news |date=December 23, 2020 |title=2020's Biggest Breakthroughs in Math and Computer Science |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HL7DEkXV_60&t=378s |work=[[Quanta Magazine]]}}</ref></blockquote>

==Recognition==
For her work on the Conway knot, Piccirillo has received several prestigious awards:

* In 2021, she was one of the inaugural recipients of the [[Breakthrough Prize#New Horizons in Mathematics Prize|Maryam Mirzakhani New Frontiers Prize]], which recognizes outstanding early-career women mathematicians.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://breakthroughprize.org/News/60|title=Winners of the 2021 Breakthrough Prizes in life sciences, fundamental physics, and mathematics announced|work=Breakthrough Prizes|date=September 10, 2020|accessdate=2020-09-19}}</ref>
* In 2021, she was awarded a [[Clay Research Fellowship]], given to recent PhDs of unusual promise,<ref>{{Cite web|title=Lisa Piccirillo |url=https://www.claymath.org/people/lisa-piccirillo/|website=Clay Mathematics Institute|accessdate=October 28, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210211143504/https://www.claymath.org/people/lisa-piccirillo/ |archive-date=11 February 2021}}</ref> and a [[Sloan Research Fellowship]], which honors "early-career researchers of outstanding promise."<ref>{{Cite web |title=2021 Fellows |url=https://sloan.org/fellowships/2021-Fellows |website=Alfred P. Sloan Foundation |access-date=2024-10-28 |archive-date=May 9, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210509113648/https://sloan.org/fellowships/2021-Fellows |url-status=dead }}</ref>

In 2020, the UK magazine ''[[Prospect (magazine)|Prospect]]'' included her on its list of "The world's top 50 thinkers for the Covid-19 age."<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.prospectmagazine.co.uk/world/40362/the-worlds-top-50-thinkers-2020|title=The world's top 50 thinkers 2020|first=Prospect|last=Team|website=www.prospectmagazine.co.uk}}</ref>
